          "h": "\nThe theme: The Four Species embodying the four letters of the Tetragrammaton, the Aravah (Arba Chayim), and the awakening of remorse in every Jew. The Four Species correspond to the four letters of the Tetragrammaton (Y-H-V-H), each being a unique wellspring of eternal life. The Etrog (taste and fragrance) corresponds to the letter Yud (Chochmah in the brain, the seat of the pure Neshamah where evil has no grasp), equaling Torah with the kollel. The Hadas (fragrance without taste) corresponds to the upper Hei (Binah in the heart, spiritual fragrance enjoyed by the soul, Berachos 43b), equaling Chayim with the kollel (69), the fountainhead of life. The Lulav (taste without fragrance) corresponds to the letter Vav (the straight spine of Yaakov's truth extending into the six extremities), being the tallest species because action is manifest. The Aravah (neither taste nor fragrance) corresponds to the final letter Hei (Knesset Israel / Malchus), whose numerical root Arav equals four times Chayim (ע-ר-ב = 272 = 4 × 68), while the Hei alludes to the final Hei. The final Hei has an open lower foot through which one can stumble toward death; yet its upper portal remains open for repentance. Every Jew from the seed of the Patriarchs experiences moments of sincere remorse (charatah) in his lifetime; even if transient, that holy spark of the soul’s root never perishes, entering through the upper aperture of the Hei to ascend to the place where penitents stand."

          "h": "\nThe theme: Sukkah as the shadow of faith (Tzila d'Mehemnuta) for the native-born, the exemption of slaves, and the maternal wing of Imma Tata'ah. The festival of Succos was given unto the native-born in Israel (kol ha-ezrach b'Yisrael yeshvu va-sukkot, Vayikra 23:42), rooted in the holy stock. The eschatological test of the nations will be the mitzvah of Sukkah (Avodah Zarah 3a), and their failure to ascend on Succos will constitute their future punishment (Zechariah 14:16–19), for the nations possess no affinity with this holy joy or eternal life. Even the pious of the nations who earn a portion in the World to Come will exist as servants unto Israel; currently their worship is directed through intermediaries (\"which Hashem your God has allotted unto all the nations\", Devarim 4:19). A slave is halachically exempt from Sukkah (Sukkah 8b), because the Sukkah is the shadow of faith (Tzila d'Mehemnuta, Zohar III, 103a) and protection under Hashem's shadow, belonging exclusively to those who have no master other than Hashem. Israel was redeemed from Egypt to be His servants alone (\"for they are My servants\", Vayikra 25:55). The Sechach in the wilderness, grown from the earth and impervious to ritual defilement, reflects \"Truth springs out of the earth\" (Tehillim 85:12)—the level of Yaakov whose bed is whole. The Sukkah is Imma Tata'ah hovering with her protective wings over all the souls of Israel: even a rebellious son remains a child of Yaakov, an attachment that can never be severed, qualifying him to rejoice in the season of our gladness."

          "h": "\nThe theme: Numerical mysteries of Sukkah, the nullification of the Sitra d'Muta (480), and the contrast between Yosef and Yehudah. The word Sukkah (סֻכָּה = 91) equals the two divine Names Y-H-V-H (26) and A-D-N-Y (65), uniting the Holy One and His Shechinah (Vav-Hei / Yaakov and Knesset Israel). The defective spelling Sukkat (סֻכַּת = 480) with the four letters equals seven times Chayim (7 × 68 = 476 + 4 = 480), corresponding to the seven lower Sefirot, the seven days of the festival, and the seven Clouds of Glory. This total of 480 counteracts and abolishes the Sitra d'Muta—the unholy feminine shell of death which likewise equals 480 (לִילִית = 480)—which brought mourning into the world, whereas Succos is consummate joy. Therefore, \"our father Jacob never died\" (Ta'anit 5b), for within him is the root of Succos, the wellspring of eternal life. Sukkot spelled fully with Yaakov spelled with a Vav (סוכות יעקוב = 496 + 182 = 678, with the two words = 680) equals ten times Chayim (10 × 68 = 680), representing the ten Sefirot. In contrast, the covenant of Bris (בְּרִית = 612) equals nine times Chayim (9 × 68 = 612), representing the ninth Sefirah, Yesod. Torah (611) with the kollel likewise equals nine times Chayim (612), for it is the ninth Sefirah from below (Chochmah). Torah study ascends from below to Above, whereas fighting the yetzer descends from Above to below into the darkest rungs. The letter Tet (ט = 9) signifies Tov (good), the 9th letter, mirroring the Tzaddik and Torah. Yosef represents the first nine Sefirot (Yehosef possessing Yud-Hei-Vav, Tehillim 81:6); while Yehudah encompasses the entire Tetragrammaton with the letter Dalet representing humility, which receiving the embryo transforms into the fertile Hei, attaining the Crown of Royalty."

        {
          "h": "The theme: The future unification of Ephraim and Yehudah, the letter Vav of truth, and Eliyahu the peacemaker. In the Future, the Holy One will make Yehudah and Yosef into \"one tree\" (Yechezkel 37:19), when Ephraim shall no longer envy Yehudah (Yeshayah 11:13), recognizing Yehudah's royal preeminence. All ten Sefirotic rungs will then be perfected throughout Israel, all being designated Yehudim after Yehudah. In this world of falsehood the truth is concealed, wherefore truth was cast to the ground (Bereishis Rabbah 8:5); yet Israel possesses the concealed letter Vav of Yaakov (Ya'akov spelled with a Vav five times in Scripture, matching the five times Eliyahu is spelled defectively without a Vav, Rashi on Vayikra 26:42). Yaakov took the Vav as a pledge from Eliyahu—the unique individual who never sinned and lives forever—to guarantee that he would come to herald the redemption when all Israel is refined to be like him. Eliyahu did not produce offspring (Zohar Chadash); having no physical progeny, the Vav was manifest within him individually. Yet because collective Israel was not yet perfected, Eliyahu's name was diminished five times, corresponding to the five soul-levels: Nefesh, Ruach, Neshamah, Chayah, and Yechidah. When Eliyahu arrives to establish peace, even the destitute in Israel will be exalted like Eliyahu (Shir HaShirim Rabbah 7:6). Peace was never cast to the ground, only Truth (Bereishis Rabbah 8:5); all strife and division in this world stem solely from the concealment of truth, mortals disputing what is genuinely true and good."

          "h": "The theme: The schism between Yehudah and Yosef, cutting the shoots (kotzetz ba-netiot), and the completion of Succos on Hoshanah Rabbah. The historical discord between Yehudah and Yosef and the division of the Davidic monarchy by Jeroboam of the tribe of Ephraim stemmed from the imperfection of this world, where no man is wholly righteous without sin (Koheles 7:20). Neither had yet attained consummate perfection in both Torah scholarship and saintly piety: each grasped nine Sefirot. Tikkunei Zohar (Tikkun 70) teaches that one who grasps nine Sefirot without Malchus \"cuts down the shoots\" (kotzetz ba-netiot), whence issue all forms of idolatry—the sin of Jeroboam and the kings of Israel, which infected the House of David through the intermarriage of Yehoshaphat with the house of Ahab (II Divrei HaYamim 18:1). This precipitated the destruction of the First Temple, until the Men of the Great Assembly nullified the inclination for idolatry (Yoma 69b). Yet the inclination for sexual immorality remained, breeding Sadducees and heretics who grasp Malchus without the upper nine Sefirot, denying the Root (kofer ba-ikar). In the footsteps of the Messiah (ikvesa d'Meshicha), insolence will increase (chutza yisgeh, Sotah 49b), insolence being \"sovereignty without a crown\" (malchuta b'lo taga, Sanhedrin 105a). Because Israel is not yet unified, unrestrained laughter is forbidden in this world (Berachos 31a). A foretaste of perfect joy is experienced on Succos, culminating on Hoshanah Rabbah (the Day of the Aravah, completing seven times Chayim and rectifying even the transgressors of Israel), advancing unto Shemini Atzeret and Simchat Torah."

          "h": "The theme: Remembering Amalek in exile, cooling the holy fervor (asher karcha), and spiritual sluggishness as the root of sin. The commandment to blot out Amalek applies when Hashem grants rest from enemies (Devarim 25:19); what benefit is there in remembering Amalek during exile? Scripture states: \"how he met you (asher karcha) by the way\" (ibid. 25:18)—meaning he cooled you (heikarcha) before others (Rashi). After the miracles of Egypt, all nations feared to touch Israel until Amalek, \"first of the nations,\" jumped into the boiling cauldron, cooling the awe of Hashem. This mirrors the primeval Serpent who opened with: \"Yea, has God said (af ki amar Elokim)?\" (Bereishis 3:1), trivializing the command to cool holy trembling. External warfare issues from internal spiritual warfare: as man subdues the yetzer within, so are external enemies vanquished. At Sinai, freedom from the yetzer brought freedom from imperial subjugation (Eruvin 54a). Amalek’s primary tactic is not to incite blatant transgression immediately, but to cool the warmth of the Jewish heart toward Torah and mitzvos, injecting lethargy (atzlut) to extinguish alacrity (zerizut). He strikes first at the \"feeble behind you\" (necheshalim)—those already sluggish—and then spreads exhaustion through the entire camp (\"and you were faint and weary\", Devarim 25:18). Sluggishness in divine service is the inception of all spiritual decline (\"the beginning of falling is flight\", Sotah 44b). Carnal lusts rule only in a heart empty of Torah (Rambam, Issurei Biah 22:21; Yevamos 63b); when Amalek injects laziness into Torah study, the innate yetzer hara seizes the opportunity to pursue selfish gratification."

          "h": "The theme: Amalek severing the circumcision, the alliance of Balaam and Amalek (Keser and Da'as of the husk), and Moshe raising his hands in prayer. Scripture records: \"and smote the hindmost of you (va-yzenav becha)\" (Devarim 25:18), which Chazal interpret: Amalek severed the circumcisions of Israel and cast them heavenward, crying: \"Take what You have chosen!\" (Tanchuma, Ki Teitzei §9; Pesikta Rabbati §12). The sign of the covenant testifies that Israel is holy; even uncircumcised Israelites are legally called circumcised (Nedarim 31b), a paradox the nations cannot comprehend. Balaam’s eye was blinded because he could not understand how cohabitation could be holy when people also derive pleasure, joining Amalek to prosecute that Israel's stragglers were motivated by physical desire. Balaam and Amalek are one rung in evil: Amalek is Keser of the husk, while Balaam (\"who knows the knowledge of the Most High\", Bamidbar 24:16) is Da'as of the husk. In holiness, Moshe is the internal Da'as and Yaakov is the external garment (Moshe milgao, Ya'akov milbar, Tikkunei Zohar, Tikkun 13). When Moshe held up his hand, Israel prevailed (Shemos 17:11): elevating Da'as to its root in Keser Elyon causes Israel to look heavenward and subjugate their hearts to their Father in Heaven (Rosh Hashanah 29a), dispelling Amalek's coldness and sluggishness. \"And it came to pass (Va-yehi)\" signifies joy (Bereishis Rabbah 42:3); \"and it shall be when Hashem has given you rest (ve-hayah b'hani'ach)... you shall blot out Amalek\" (Devarim 25:19) teaches that blotting out Amalek is achieved through the joy of a mitzvah (simchah shel mitzvah), which fills the heart with alacrity. Remembering Amalek in every generation elevates the mind to its primordial root, shattering Amalek's power."

          "h": "\nThe theme: Amalek severing the circumcision, the alliance of Balaam and Amalek (Keser and Da'as of the husk), and Moshe raising his hands in prayer. Scripture records: \"and smote the hindmost of you (va-yzenav becha)\" (Devarim 25:18), which Chazal interpret: Amalek severed the circumcisions of Israel and cast them heavenward, crying: \"Take what You have chosen!\" (Tanchuma, Ki Teitzei §9; Pesikta Rabbati §12). The sign of the covenant testifies that Israel is holy; even uncircumcised Israelites are legally called circumcised (Nedarim 31b), a paradox the nations cannot comprehend. Balaam’s eye was blinded because he could not understand how cohabitation could be holy when people also derive pleasure, joining Amalek to prosecute that Israel's stragglers were motivated by physical desire. Balaam and Amalek are one rung in evil: Amalek is Keser of the husk, while Balaam (\"who knows the knowledge of the Most High\", Bamidbar 24:16) is Da'as of the husk. In holiness, Moshe is the internal Da'as and Yaakov is the external garment (Moshe milgao, Ya'akov milbar, Tikkunei Zohar, Tikkun 13). When Moshe held up his hand, Israel prevailed (Shemos 17:11): elevating Da'as to its root in Keser Elyon causes Israel to look heavenward and subjugate their hearts to their Father in Heaven (Rosh Hashanah 29a), dispelling Amalek's coldness and sluggishness. \"And it came to pass (Va-yehi)\" signifies joy (Bereishis Rabbah 42:3); \"and it shall be when Hashem has given you rest (ve-hayah b'hani'ach)... you shall blot out Amalek\" (Devarim 25:19) teaches that blotting out Amalek is achieved through the joy of a mitzvah (simchah shel mitzvah), which fills the heart with alacrity. Remembering Amalek in every generation elevates the mind to its primordial root, shattering Amalek's power."

          "h": "The theme: Remembering Shabbat vs. remembering Amalek, Yehoshua and Moshe subduing the yetzer, and forgetfulness as Amalek’s weapon. Remembering the Sabbath day to sanctify it awakens the primordial holiness of Creation over a full platter of blessing; remembering Amalek is enacted over an empty platter (Midrash Tanchuma, Ki Teitzei §10)—when the heart is chilled and empty of holy desire. Yehoshua from the seed of Yosef (the master of sexual purity in deed) is the victor in physical battle; Moshe (the intellect of Israel) is the victor through Da'as, whence divine action expands. While the nations sink into an entire stature of evil issuing from Amalek and guided by Balaam's advice of licentiousness, Israel immediately arouses the good inclination against the evil inclination (Berachos 5a), preventing sin from becoming an ingrained guest (ore'ach). Although this does not eradicate evil completely—as indicated by \"and Joshua weakened (va-yacholosh) Amalek\" (Shemos 17:13)—it diminishes its power until the future rest (be-hani'ach). At Sinai, Israel became free from imperial servitude and the inborn yetzer hara inherited from the Serpent; in the Future, the Divine Name will be complete, pronounced exactly as written (Pesachim 50a). In this world, the primary remedy is holy remembrance against Amalek's forgetfulness, which distracts man into amassing worldly wealth rather than laboring in Torah and mitzvos for Hashem's glory."

          "h": "The theme: The mitzvah of Tzitzit as a physical reminder against lust, the promise of the future redemption, and man as a \"walker\" (holech) vs. angels as \"standers\" (omedim). The physical mitzvah of Tzitzit (\"that you may remember... and not seek after your own heart\", Bamidbar 15:39) does not banish lust from entering the heart, but prompts immediate rejection, like the disciple whose Tzitzit slapped him across the face, preventing sin (Menachos 44a). When the yetzer has not yet incited blatant sin but merely chills holy desire, the remedy is remembering what Amalek did—knowing that weariness in divine service is the counsel of the nations—and rejoicing in Hashem's promise that Amalek will be completely blotted out (tamcheh). Just as past sanctifications leave an eternal imprint, so future redemptions project an impression (reshimu) into the present, enabling the soul to endure the crushing burden of exile, like a bride reading her marriage contract (ketubah) to sustain her during her groom's absence (Pesikta d'Rav Kahana). The 70 nations correspond to the 70 faculties of the soul, but Amalek does not seek subjugation; his sole aim is to cool the heart’s devotion to Heaven. Man is a \"walker\" (holech), constantly moving from level to level through free choice and overcoming the yetzer, unlike angels who are \"standers\" (omedim, Zechariah 3:7) fixed in their station. \"Whoever is greater than his fellow, his yetzer is greater\" (Sukkah 52a); every ascent requires an opposing struggle, and only one whose heart is a void (chalal) without a yetzer (like David, Bava Batra 17a) ceases to fight."

          "h": "The theme: Descent for the sake of ascent (yeridah l'tzorech aliyah), the war of Amalek vs. the war of Gog, and the permutation of V-H-Y-H (ו-ה-י-ה). When a tzaddik reaches the ultimate perfection of his stature, his soul departs the world and ascends above the ministering angels, granted \"free access among these that stand by\" (mahlechim bein ha-omedim, Zechariah 3:7); \"righteous men have no rest, neither in this world nor in the World to Come, going from strength to strength\" (Berachos 64a). The moment of temptation between rungs is the descent for the sake of ascent (yeridah l'tzorech aliyah): \"a righteous man falls seven times, and rises up again\" (Mishlei 24:16). This was Rephidim: on their march to Sinai, their hands slackened from Torah, precipitating the assault of Amalek. The Zohar (II, 65b) teaches that no war in cosmic history compares to Amalek—not even the war of Gog and Magog—for it struck across all sides of the Holy One (be-chol sitrei d'Kudsha Brikh Hu). Gog will be the final war at the \"heel\" (ikvesa d'Meshicha) when the nations accuse Israel; but Amalek attacked at the very beginning of the nation's entry under the wings of the Shechinah, before Sinai unified Israel with Hashem. Before Sinai, Amalek had the power to separate the Holy One from His Shechinah, wherefore \"Hashem has a war with Amalek from generation to generation\" (Shemos 17:16), the Divine Name (Yud-Hei) and Throne (K-S) remaining incomplete until Amalek is blotted out. To destroy Amalek, the divine permutation V-H-Y-H (ו-ה-י-ה) is formed, where sons precede fathers, embodied in Moshe raising his hands to Keser Elyon. In the Purim Megillah, remembering with the mouth (the lowest rung) unites with the brain of memory (the highest rung), binding the final Hei unto the Yud and its supernal thorn, rectifying the cosmos."

          "h": "The theme: Why Purim was not established as a full Yom Tov, Chanukah vs. Purim regarding writing, and hidden vs. revealed miracles. The Sages initially sought to establish Purim as a full festival (Yom Tov) with prohibition of labor, but Israel did not accept it (Megillah 5b). A Yom Tov is termed \"Shabbat\" because it requires cessation from labor, providing rest from worldly toil, mirroring the World to Come (\"a day that is entirely Shabbat\", Tamid 7:4; Avodah Zarah 3a). Shabbat is a foretaste of the World to Come (Berachos 57a); on festivals, Israel’s sanctification (Yisrael d'kadshinhu l'zmanei) draws down supernal light through miracles that transcend nature. On Purim, Scripture uses the phrase \"and rest (ve-no'ach) from their enemies\" (Esther 9:16), a term reserved for complete rest reflecting the World to Come. Unlike Chanukah—which was not permitted to be written down in the biblical canon (Yoma 29a)—Purim was given to be inscribed in the Megillah. Writing represents open revelation accessible to all eyes, like the Written Torah, whereas oral transmission represents inner secrets (mistorin, Midrash Tanchuma, Ki Tisa §34). Chanukah was not written because its military victory was disguised in nature: few vanquished many, but the nations attributed it to Hasmonean military prowess, as later battles recorded in Sefer Yosippon were sometimes lost. Chanukah belongs to hidden daily miracles (\"and for Your miracles that are with us daily\"), perceived only through the inner recognition of the heart."

        {
          "h": "The theme: Esther as the end of all miracles, the natural garment of Purim, and the reversal of \"joy and banquet\" to \"banquet and joy.\" The Talmud states: \"Esther is the end of all miracles\" (Yoma 29a), acting as the intermediary nexus between two cosmic epochs. The miracle of Purim was cloaked within the natural order: the king repealed the decree out of love for his queen. Therefore, the Men of the Great Assembly initially hesitated to record the Megillah, arguing: \"You will arouse the jealousy and hatred of the nations against us\" (Megillah 7a). Esther responded: \"I am already recorded in the chronicles of Media and Persia\" (ibid.), for even the heathen recognized that Vashti's sudden execution and the rise of an unknown maiden (with an olive-green complexion upon whom a thread of grace was drawn, Megillah 13a) was providential, causing many to convert out of dread (mit-yahadim, Esther 8:17). Hence the Megillah was included in the Sacred Writings (Ketuvim). At the initial moment of salvation, Israel experienced complete rest and sought to establish Purim as a full Yom Tov, writing first: \"joy and banquet and a festival day\" (simchah u-mishteh v'yom tov, Esther 8:17), where joy stemmed from the holiness of the day. But when Yom Tov was not accepted, the order reversed to \"banquet and joy\" (mishteh v'simchah, ibid. 9:17–22), the joy being generated through the wine of the feast. A person is obligated to drink on Purim \"until he does not know\" (ad d'lo yada, Megillah 7b)—a state of intoxication where one is halachically exempt from mitzvos (Eruvin 65a) and forgets worldly burdens. On Shabbat and Yom Tov, rest comes through elevated intellect and settled consciousness (yishuv ha-da'at), having been completely liberated from the oppressor (\"servants of Hashem, not servants of Pharaoh\", Megillah 14b); but on Purim, Israel remained in the diaspora under Persian dominion (\"we are still the servants of Ahasuerus\", ibid.), the miracle not being recognized through conscious intellect."

As it is written: “For the seller shall not return to that which he has sold” (Ezekiel 7:13), i.e., Ezekiel prophesied that in the future the Jubilee Year would no longer be in effect. Now is it possible that the Jubilee had already been annulled? The halakhot of the Jubilee Year apply only when all of the tribes of Israel are settled in their respective places, which could not have happened since the exile of the ten tribes more than a century earlier, but the prophet is prophesying that it will cease only in the future. Rather, this teaches that Jeremiah brought back the ten tribes from their exile.’"

        {
          "h": "The theme: The threefold decree of Haman (destroy, kill, annihilate), the bowing to the statue, and the banquet of Ahasuerus. Haman’s decree contained three verbs: \"to destroy, to kill, and to annihilate\" (le-hashmid, la-harog, u-l'abed, Esther 3:13). Haman's primary desire was \"to annihilate\" (l'abed)—to assimilate Israel among the nations and destroy their distinct identity, like the lost ones in Assyria (ha-ovdim b'eretz Ashur, Yeshayah 27:13; Makkot 24a). Haman was the pioneer of forced apostasy (shemad). The decree was provoked because Israel bowed to Nebuchadnezzar's golden image (Megillah 12a); although it was a secular monument (andartei, Tosafos, Kesubos 33b) and Israel complied only for outward appearance (lifnim), it constituted a public profanation of the Divine Name (chillul Hashem). To purge this, Haman decreed that they must convert (le-hashmid), those who refuse be executed (la-harog), and their children assimilated (u-l'abed), just as Amalek is denied conversion (Mechilta, Beshalach). Similarly, the opinion that Israel was punished for partaking in Ahasuerus's feast (Megillah 12a) addresses assimilation: dining together breeds intermarriage (Shabbat 17b; Chullin 4b). Though Israel attended out of fear of the king without inward desire to assimilate, it generated a chillul Hashem. When the decree was promulgated, all Israel resolved to offer their lives in sanctification of the Divine Name, ready to slaughter their children rather than surrender them to assimilation (as Ashkenazic and Sephardic martyrs did during the Crusades). This sincere willingness to die sufficed to rectify the past; because Israel's original sin was merely for outward appearance (lifnim), Hashem rescinded the decree, which had also been enacted merely for outward appearance (lifnim)."

        {
          "h": "The theme: Shushan’s extra day of vengeance, Chananya, Mishael, and Azariah, and the hidden root of the Persian decree. After repentance converted intentional sins into merits, the Jews of Shushan—who had borne the brunt of the sin of the banquet—were granted an extra day of vengeance against their enemies (the fifteenth of Adar). Executing those Persians who witnessed the chillul Hashem eradicated all memory of sin. Because the decree was merely superficial (lifnim), the miracle was likewise cloaked in nature, lacking the overt sanctity of a Yom Tov; it is grasped only in the drunkenness of ad d'lo yada, where outward distinctions blur. Why did the decree occur long after Nebuchadnezzar's statue? At the statue, Israel acted under duress; the true chillul Hashem emerged only after Chananya, Mishael, and Azariah were saved from the fiery furnace (Daniel 3), causing Israel's compliance to be condemned as cowardice (Sanhedrin 93a). Hashem is meticulous with the righteous: even when performing a great deed, a tzaddik must ensure his fellow is not punished through his superior piety. Eliyahu was compelled to revive the son of the widow of Zarephath because she argued that his intense sanctity caused her sins to be remembered (I Melachim 17:18). When Chananya, Mishael, and Azariah were punished (drowning in spit, Sanhedrin 93a), accepting death for all Israel, their sacrifice protected the generation, arousing profound sanctification of the Divine Name."

        {
          "h": "The theme: Israel as a complete corporate stature, the legacy of Chananya, Mishael, and Azariah (shevak lan chayim), and the calculation of the seventy years. Israel constitutes a single corporate stature with heads, eyes, and organs; Chananya, Mishael, and Azariah were the inward depths of the heart of Knesset Israel in their generation. Intrinsically, no Jew desired to bow to the statue; yet because it was an imperial monument (andartei), the Torah did not mandate martyrdom (Tosafos, Kesubos 33b). When the three youths demonstrated actual martyrdom, their holiness was not yet deeply anchored throughout the entire nation. Had all Israel offered their lives then, they would have been redeemed immediately from Nebuchadnezzar's yoke; but the decreed seventy years of exile had not yet expired. When a tzaddik passes, he leaves his vitality (shevak lan chayim) to become permanently integrated within Israel, as hinted in Koheles Rabbah (12:11): \"the words of the wise are as goads—when are they as goads? When their masters are gathered from them.\" Through their death, the capacity for martyrdom spread throughout all Israel, though remaining dormant until the decree of Ahasuerus. Ahasuerus calculated that the seventy years of Jeremiah's prophecy had concluded without redemption, celebrating his banquet with Temple vessels (Megillah 12a). Had Israel possessed sufficient merit, the seventy years could have been reckoned according to Ahasuerus's count and the redemption would have unfolded then, just as Daniel's prophecies of the End remain sealed to depend upon the merits of each generation."

As it is written with regard to Jeremiah’s prophecy of a return to Eretz Yisrael: “After seventy years are accomplished for Babylonia I will remember you and perform My good word toward you, enabling you to return to this place” (Jeremiah 29:10), and elsewhere it is written in a slightly different formulation: “In the first year of his reign, I, Daniel, meditated in the books, over the number of the years, which the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah the prophet, that He would accomplish for the desolations of Jerusalem seventy years” (Daniel 9:2).           "h": "\nThe theme: Ahasuerus's banquet as a trial of martyrdom, the Sanhedrin as \"eyes of the congregation\", and the dual perspective on drinking gentile wine. The banquet of Ahasuerus was divinely arranged to bring Israel into a trial of martyrdom (mesirat nefesh) by abstaining from attendance. Had they offered their lives to avoid going, their latent power of martyrdom would have been actualized, and the seventy years of Jeremiah's prophecy would have been completed then. Although this test centered in Shushan, the Great Sanhedrin was located there—as the Sanhedrin resided in the royal capital in Israel and in exile (for \"who are kings? The Rabbis\", Gittin 62a). Mordechai and the Sanhedrin were present, expounded in Megillah (12b) on the verse \"to the wise men who knew the times\" (Esther 1:13). The Sanhedrin is termed the \"eyes of the congregation\" (einei ha-eidah, Bamidbar 15:24); desire begins with the seeing eye, after which the heart covets. As the Talmud states: \"A bride whose eyes are beautiful requires no examination of her body\" (Ta'anis 24a); had the Sanhedrin stood firm, all Israel would have been validated. Because their eyes faltered, the entire nation required testing, reawakening the heavenly accusation regarding the golden image. Strictly speaking, attending the feast was not halachically one of the three cardinal sins requiring martyrdom; according to the Rambam (Hilchos Yesodei HaTorah 5:4), giving up one's life when not mandated is forbidden. Yet here was an emergency hour to act for Hashem (es la'asos la-Hashem). Attending a gentile banquet involves the fringe of idolatry: \"Israelites in the diaspora worship idols in purity—how so? When a gentile makes a feast... and they eat of their own\" (Avodah Zarah 8a). Mordechai and the Sanhedrin believed that by attending and strictly eating their own kosher food under royal decree (\"to do according to every man's pleasure\", Esther 1:8), they would publicly demonstrate Israel's distinct holiness. While their intention was purely for Heaven, they erred in underestimating the fringe of idolatry caused by Ahasuerus's pagan thanksgiving, satisfying the malicious desire of Haman who judged merely by outward appearance."

        {
          "h": "\nThe theme: The decree of \"no compulsion\", the test of subtle prohibitions, the fear of the king as a subtle bribe, and the cure before the blow (refuah kodemet la-makah). The decree that \"none did compel\" (Esther 1:8) was instituted so that each nation could act according to its customs; thus Israel’s kosher dining did not stand out as an act of divine defiance, but appeared merely as compliance with royal decree. An unqualified \"king\" in the Megillah refers homiletically to the King of kings (Zohar III, 109a): the Holy One brought Israel to a test in a matter that was not a blatant biblical prohibition, for to eat forbidden foods the righteous would have gladly accepted martyrdom. The test was in an ambiguous matter where error was possible, appearing as complete purity. Yet had their hearts been entirely free from fear of the king, the Sanhedrin would have correctly expounded Rabbi Yishmael’s ruling forbidding attendance. Subtle fear of the monarch acted as a subconscious bribe (shochad) that blinds the eyes of the wise (Devarim 16:19). Although they strengthened themselves in the fear of Hashem, they were still subjects under Ahasuerus's rule. This subtle fear caused the decree to descend upon all Israel, whose eyes (the Sanhedrin) were imperfect. Yet because their intention was pure, the decree was likewise merely superficial (lifnim). At that very banquet, Hashem prepared the cure before the blow (refuah kodemet la-makah, Megillah 13b) through the execution of Vashti, when the King consulted the \"wise men who knew the times\"—an allegorical trial in the Heavenly Court regarding Israel's salvation."

          "h": "\nThe theme: Haman's lottery, the death vs. birth of Moshe in Adar, and Israel's mastery over time. Haman cast lots from month to month (Esther 3:7) because he knew that certain times are astrologically prepared for calamity (Sanhedrin 102a). Recognizing that he could not vanquish Israel through legal prosecution on High, he sought an auspicious hour for catastrophe. The Ninth of Av is designated for national weeping (Ta'anis 29a), but not for annihilation; in truth, no time exists for Israel's destruction, for heaven and earth were created for their sake (Bereishis Rabbah 1:4). Haman calculated that Moshe died in Adar, when the fountains of wisdom were sealed and the flow of the Written Torah ceased. The nations grasp only the Written Torah, which is open to all; they have no part in the Oral Torah, which is Hashem's secret mystery (mistorin, Tanchuma, Ki Tisa §34). Haman assumed that Moshe's death marked the permanent cessation of Torah, but was ignorant that Moshe was likewise born in Adar (Megillah 13b), an auspicious sign for the renewal of Torah through voluntary re-acceptance (hadar kibluha bi-yemei Achashverosh, Shabbat 88a). Haman thought like pagan astrologers who believe a time can possess only a single predetermined quality. The nations are subjugated to time; Israel is above time, governing time because Hashem entrusted the calendar unto the earthly court (\"this month shall be unto you\", Shemos 12:2; Rosh Hashanah 22a). On Tisha B'Av weeping was decreed because the generation of the wilderness despised the Holy Land; Moshe's death in Adar was not on account of sin, but because Hashem completes the years of the righteous from day to day (Rosh Hashanah 11a). \"Better is the day of death than the day of one's birth\" (Koheles 7:1): at death, a tzaddik's soul ascends, bequeathing the capacity for Torah understanding into the inward depths of every Jewish heart as the foundation of the Oral Torah."

          "h": "\nThe theme: The cancellation of Torah as its foundation (bitulah shel Torah zehu yisudah), Otniel ben Kenaz, and the cessation of prophecy. The Oral Torah began after Moshe's death: during the days of mourning for Moshe, three hundred halachot were forgotten (Temurah 16a), but the Sages taught that \"the suspension of Torah study is its very foundation\" (Menachos 99a). Through the forgetting of these laws, Otniel ben Kenaz toiled in rigorous analytical argumentation (pilpul) and restored them (Temurah 16a). This inaugurated the Oral Torah—attaining divine truth through the Holy Spirit within the Sages (Bava Batra 12a; Ramban). The nations presumed that Moshe's death marked the end of the Torah, but in truth it was the birth of the Oral Law; Haman's decree likewise became the foundation for Israel re-accepting the Torah (kiyyemu ve-kiblu, Shabbat 88a). The foundational era of the Oral Torah was established by the Men of the Great Assembly, the authors of rabbinic enactments, fences (seyag la-Torah), and hermeneutic principles (Avos 1:1). As prophecy ceased, Haman sensed that the era of direct revelation had closed and that the canon of biblical scripture was sealed; but he did not know that \"the words of the Scribes are more beloved than the wine of the Torah\" (Avodah Zarah 35a). Divine revelation is greatest specifically within deep concealment: \"He has set me in dark places—this is the Babylonian Talmud\" (Eichah 3:6; Sanhedrin 24a), whose cryptic debates conceal the mysteries of Torah. Moshe is the collective Da'as of Israel (the \"generation of knowledge\", dor de'ah), Da'as being the Holy Spirit. His death was the concealment of explicit Da'as, leading to the requirement of drinking on Purim \"until he does not know\" (ad d'lo yada). Haman assumed that the cessation of Da'as was permanent, unaware that Adar was the month of Moshe's birth and the inception of transcendent revelation through concealment."

          "h": "\nThe theme: Purim as illumination in the absence of Da'as, wisdom among the nations vs. Torah in Israel, and the prophecy of Balaam. Israel originally sought to establish Purim as a full Yom Tov, believing that through their own merit they had sanctified time; but when it was revealed that their deliverance was cloaked in nature (lifnim), they recognized that the time remained in the concealment of Da'as. Yet Israel perceives divine truth even in the absence of conscious intellect (ad d'lo yada). While the nations possess human wisdom regarding which a blessing is recited (\"Blessed is He Who gave of His wisdom to flesh and blood\", Berachos 58a; Megillah 16a), \"if a person says to you: there is wisdom among the nations, believe him; if he says: there is Torah among the nations, do not believe him\" (Eichah Rabbah 2:13). Torah is Da'as—the influx of the Holy Spirit from Chochmah Ila'ah, which belongs exclusively to Israel. In this world, the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil creates an external counterfeit for everything: opposite Moshe's Da'as, Balaam arose boasting \"who knows the knowledge of the Most High\" (Bamidbar 24:16; Sifrei, Devarim §357). Moshe requested that the Shechinah never rest upon the nations, which was fulfilled upon his passing (Berachos 7a; Bava Batra 15b); thereafter, direct prophecy departed from the nations. The wisdom of the gentiles is human intellect, whose ultimate truth consists in recognizing Israel's supremacy, as Balaam foresaw and as the nations will demonstrate in the Future, ten men grasping the corner of a Jew's garment to serve him (Zechariah 8:23). Haman's wise counselors recognized this in his final hour, perceiving that if Mordechai is of the seed of the Jews, Haman is doomed to fall (Esther 6:13)."

          "h": "The theme: Moshe writing the final eight verses with tears, the cessation of prophecy of Torah laws, and Israel's mastery over astronomical time. Before his death, Moshe fulfilled the final commandment of writing a Sefer Torah, writing thirteen scrolls for each tribe and the Ark (Midrash Tehillim 90:3; Yerushalmi Sotah 5:6). A Torah scroll lacking a single letter is invalid (Menachos 29b); hence Moshe wrote the final eight verses depicting his death with tears (b'dema, Bava Batra 15a) as his soul departed, concluding the Pentateuch. From then on, \"it is not in heaven\" (Devarim 30:12)—no further direct legislative revelation descended from Heaven in this world. Prophecy thereafter served solely to admonish Israel to observe the Torah and to foretell the future. The nations counterpart to this is astrology (itzganinut); gentiles tremble before celestial omens (Yirmiyah 10:2), but Israel does not, for the stars govern time, and the nations are under time (tachat ha-zman). Israel is above time (l'ma'lah min ha-zman); Hashem alters planetary orbits at will, as He told Avraham regarding Jupiter (Tzedek, Shabbat 156b). When prophecy ceased, it was replaced by the intense expansion of the Oral Torah (Torah she-b'al Peh), re-accepted out of love in the days of Ahasuerus (Shabbat 88a; Midrash Tanchuma, Noach §3). Prophecy emanates from Netzach and Hod, whereas the Holy Spirit (Ruach HaKodesh) of the Sages is hewn from supernal Chochmah, transcending the prophecy of all prophets. In the First Temple, righteous leaders craved the explicit clarity of prophecy; in the Second Temple, despite the absence of the Shechinah, the splendor of Torah culminated in the deep, nocturnal secrets (mistorin) of the Oral Law (Sefer Heichalot)."

        {
          "h": "The theme: Haman anticipating the end of prophecy, the descent of pagan sorcery to the feet of death, and the Greek philosophical denial of the occult. Haman—perceiving through his astrologers who see but do not understand—sensed that he was destined to trigger the cessation of prophecy. He sought to seal divine vision entirely by destroying the Torah, assuming that Adar, the month of Moshe's passing, was propitious for this. When prophecy existed in Israel to reveal the future, an unholy parallel existed among the nations through astrology, divination, and witchcraft. Yet while prophecy issued from the word of Hashem, it was not the legislative Torah from supernal Chochmah, descending from the lower attributes at the level of the \"feet\" (raglin). The feet descend to the realm of death (\"her feet go down to death\", Mishlei 5:5; ve-Atah mechayeh et kulam, Nechemyah 9:6), whence the nations derived their occult vitality. When counsel was lost from the children of Israel, gentile divination rotted as well (\"is counsel perished from the prudent? is their wisdom vanished?\", Yirmiyah 49:7). At the beginning of the Greek empire prophecy departed (Seder Olam Rabbah §30), and the foundation of the Oral Torah was laid. In counterpoint, Greek philosophy and rationalism arose, denying astrology, sorcery, and everything transcending human intellect. In Israel, true wisdom is the attainment of the Holy Spirit, enabling sages to know the future through Torah wisdom, as Rabban Gamliel perceived through the Holy Spirit (Eruvin 64b). Torah wisdom recognizes that authentic truth transcends mortal logic; hence Jewish sages are called \"knowers of the times\" (yod'ei ha-ittim), whereas among the nations, philosophers and astrologers are two divided disciplines."

        {
          "h": "The theme: The royal decree to \"all who know religion and law\" (Dat va-Din), and the Jewish Sanhedrin as masters who establish time. Scripture states: \"for so was the king's manner toward all that knew law and judgment (dat va-din)\" (Esther 1:13). Dat is legislation enacted by authorities possessing knowledge transcending human intellect; Din is rational jurisprudence based on human logic. Ancient nations judged civil matters by rational logic (din) while consulting oracles, soothsayers, and idols for suprarational statutes (dat). Haman said of Israel: \"their laws (dateyhem) are diverse from all people\" (Esther 3:8), because the Torah is suprarational divine wisdom; \"neither keep they the king's laws (datei ha-melech)\" (ibid.) refers to imperial whims that defy human reason, unlike civil taxes which fall under dina d'malchuta dina (Gittin 10b). Ahasuerus consulted \"the wise men who knew the times\" (Esther 1:13)—which Chazal identify as the Jewish Sanhedrin, combining wisdom and knowledge of the times in a single title. While gentile astrologers merely report what they see in the stars, the Sages of Israel arrange time itself, the calendar being committed to their jurisdiction to intercalate years and sanctify months. Ahasuerus questioned whether Vashti was liable to execution according to Torah wisdom (Chochmah) and whether the propitious moment (Et) had arrived to execute a queen. Heaven orchestrated this so the Sanhedrin would arouse the remedy before the blow. The Sages who attended the feast initially erred; but following their stumble, their hearts smote them (like David in I Shmuel 24:5; Alshich), returning to Hashem with full repentance and awakening the divine cure."

Therefore, I retract my previous statement and say that although the Sages said that in the case of one who betroths half a woman, she is not betrothed, however, if there was a half-maidservant half-free woman who was betrothed, then her betrothal is a valid betrothal. What is the reason for the distinction? There, he left a portion of the woman out of his acquisition; here, he did not leave a portion of the woman out of his acquisition.’"

        {
          "h": "The theme: Hashem consulting the Sages, Memuchan digging his own pit, and the limit of gentile foresight. The King of kings consulted the Sages of Israel regarding Vashti just as He consulted the souls of the righteous prior to creating Man (\"Let us make man\", Bereishis Rabbah 8:7). In every generation, the eminent Torah leaders constitute the Heavenly Court on Earth: Hashem does nothing without their counsel, the righteous ruling in the fear of God with power to annul divine decrees (Moed Katan 16b; Bereishis 18:17). The time had arrived for the rebuilding of the Second Temple at the close of Jeremiah's seventy years. Recognizing that they had sinned by attending the banquet, the Sanhedrin refused to rule based on their personal Torah merit; instead, they invoked the collective merit of the Temple sacrifices, which even simple Jews passionately yearned to restore. In the earthly court, when Ahasuerus consulted them, they recused themselves from judging Vashti, refusing to let an accuser become an advocate (ein kateigor na'aseh saneigor, Berachos 59a). Their inward repentance caused Heaven to inspire Memuchan—who is Haman (Megillah 12b)—to dig his own pit by counseling Vashti's execution, preparing his own gallows. From that moment he was called Memuchan, being prepared (muchan) for retribution. Haman was blinded by pride, whereas authentic wisdom belongs to one who foresees future consequences (eizehu chacham haro'eh et ha-nolad, Tamid 32a). Haman’s pagan astrologers possessed a trace of foresight, warning him that if Mordechai is of the seed of the Jews he would fall (Esther 6:13); yet Haman stubbornly refused to believe his own downfall, pleading for his life before Esther."

        {
          "h": "The theme: Haman's folly, his assault on Esther, the name Memuchan as mere preparation, and Shushan Purim. The Blessed Name exposed Haman's sheer foolishness: whatever he cunningly devised to elevate himself and harm others redounded to his own ruin from beginning to end. When Ahasuerus returned and exclaimed: \"Will he even force the queen before me in the house?\" (Esther 7:8), this narrative was recorded to reveal the depth of wicked depravity: even at the very threshold of Gehinnom, the wicked do not repent (Eruvin 19a). Haman threw himself upon the couch intentionally to violate and defile Esther, plotting that even if begun under duress, she would eventually succumb to unholy intimacy—as stated regarding Dinah that once a woman is defiled by an uncircumcised pagan, it is difficult to detach her (Bereishis Rabbah 80:11)—hoping to bring her under his influence to forget her people and ancestral heritage. He still refused to acknowledge that all events were divinely orchestrated for Israel's salvation, continuing to plot how to fulfill his evil schemes; in that instant his verdict was sealed for absolute destruction. Amalek is the \"first of the nations\" (reishit goyim), having power solely in the initial thought (machshavah) without the ability to actualize it into lasting deed (po'al), for had his cosmic evil actualized, the world could not endure. Thus he is called Memuchan—meaning mere preparation (hachanah) without completion, an inception devoid of an end. Through his own gallows he unwittingly prepared the cure before the blow, awakening Israel's heart to re-accept the Torah out of love; on account of this preparatory spark, his descendants merited to study Torah in Bnei Brak (Sanhedrin 96b). While the fourteenth of Adar commemorates the salvation from the decree, the fifteenth commemorates the rectification of Shushan’s feast where the cure was hatched, establishing Shushan Purim for all generations."

          "h": "The theme: The Three Decrees (destroy, kill, annihilate) countered by the Three Observances, the wine of Torah, and the Three Cardinal Sins. Against Haman's three decrees—\"to destroy, to kill, and to annihilate\" (Esther 3:13)—the Sages instituted three observances. \"Gladness and feasting\" (simchah u-mishteh) form a single continuum countering \"to destroy\" (le-hashmid), which targeted the abolition of the Torah. The Torah is compared to bread and wine: \"Come, eat of my bread, and drink of the wine which I have mingled\" (Mishlei 9:5); hence the Purim meal consists of bread and wine, given to warriors after battle. It is called mishteh after wine because a man must drink \"until he does not know\" (ad d'lo yada), representing the suspension of external intellect which is the very foundation of the Oral Torah. The salvation was seeded at Ahasuerus's banquet \"when the heart of the king was merry with wine\" (Esther 1:10): wine can lead to unholy licentiousness (Sotah 7a), but when directed toward holiness, wine makes one wise (Yoma 76b), embodying the wine of Torah (yeina shel Torah). This is the wine drunk on Purim, celebrating the voluntary re-acceptance of the Torah out of love (hadar kibluha me-ahavah, Shabbat 88a), when the secret mysteries (mistorin) of the Torah were revealed in the absence of conscious Da'as. \"The words of the Scribes are more beloved than the wine of the Torah\" (Eruvin 21b; Shir HaShirim 1:2), reflecting the intense love between Knesset Israel and Hashem. The Zohar teaches: the Torah, the Holy One, and Israel are completely one (kula chad, Zohar III, 73a). Israel is one nation believing in One God who is called the God of Israel, unified through the Torah. Opposite this stand the three cardinal sins: Idolatry denies God's oneness; Sexual Immorality is immersion in lust, the antithesis of the Torah which disciplines desire (Avos 4:4; Sanhedrin 106b); and Bloodshed destroys a soul and limb of the Israelite nation, whose collective body is one organism. Loving one's neighbor as oneself is the great principle of the Torah (Bereishis Rabbah 24:7); the souls of Israel are the actualized generations of Man, and the Torah is the book of the generations of Man (sefer toldot adam, Bereishis 5:1), all rooted in Hashem is One."

        {
          "h": "The theme: Haman targeting the three pillars, the Jewish traits of mercy and modesty, and the riddle of Rabbah slaying Rabbi Zeira. Haman plotted to uproot all three foundations: \"to destroy\" (le-hashmid) meant abolishing the Torah, assuming Israel was submerged in worldly lust at the banquet; yet it emerged that even during the feast they remained cleaved unto Hashem. \"To kill\" (la-harog) targeted the physical shedding of Israel's blood, claiming they were no longer a distinct nation. But the hallmark of Israel is the exact antithesis of bloodshed: the Gibeonites were excluded from Israel because they demanded the blood of Saul's sons (II Shmuel 21; Yevamos 79a), whereas Israelites possess three innate traits: merciful, bashful, and doers of kindness (rachmanim, bayshanim, ve-gomlei chasadim). To counter \"to kill,\" the Sages instituted Mishlo'ach Manot (love of friends) and Matanot LaEvyonim (mercy on the destitute). Even when intoxicated ad d'lo yada, the Jew's inward heart remains submerged in love of Israel. Even an act appearing like murder—such as Rabbah rising and slaughtering Rabbi Zeira at the Purim feast (Megillah 7b)—was merely an outward appearance (lifnim); Rabbah immediately prayed and revived him. The Talmud recorded this bizarre event to teach that even when a Jew appears to commit murder, it is only superficial; commentators explain that Rabbah urged Rabbi Zeira to drink excessive wine until his soul departed, acting out of intense love to gladden him. Rabbah revived him on Shushan Purim, the day rectifying the Persian banquet, demonstrating that the Holy One does not perform miracles for a lie (Kudsha Brikh Hu lo avid nisa l'shikrei)."

        {
          "h": "The theme: The Megillah countering \"to annihilate\", the omission of God's Name, and the sleepless Guardian of Israel. Against Haman's third decree, \"to annihilate\" (u-l'abed)—which intended the withdrawal of the Shechinah from terrestrial creation leaving Hashem merely the \"God of heaven\" (Elaha d'Elaha, Menachos 110a)—stands the public reading of the Megillah (Mikra Megillah), publicizing the miracle (pirsumei nisa) so that all the ends of the earth behold the salvation of our God (Megillah 11a). \"Light\" (Orah) is Torah, countering \"to destroy\"; \"gladness and a festival day\" (Sason v'Yom Tov)—circumcision and sanctifying time—counters \"to kill\", manifesting Israel as \"one nation.\" Circumcision at eight days is an inborn sanctity received after passing through a Shabbat (Vayikra Rabbah 27:10), a fixed holiness forbidden unto pagans (Sanhedrin 59a). \"Honor\" (Yakar) is Tefillin, manifesting \"Hashem is One,\" so that all nations see that Hashem's Name is called upon Israel (Devarim 28:10). Megillah denotes revelation (gilui); yet no explicit Divine Name appears in the Megillah, for the essential revelation of Purim is that even when Israel appears abandoned in the diaspora, it is merely superficial (lifnim). Haman claimed that Israel was asleep from the mitzvos and that their God was asleep as well; but Knesset Israel responds: \"I sleep, but my heart wakes\" (Shir HaShirim 5:2)—the Holy One being the sleepless heart of Israel (\"Behold, He that keeps Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep\", Tehillim 121:4). The apparent sleep of the Babylonian exile existed only for mortal eyes; Hashem looks into the heart where His presence burns brightly, turning Haman's schemes entirely to the contrary (ve-nahafoch hu)."

        {
          "h": "The theme: The festival of Rosh Hashanah, \"convening of holiness\" (mikra kodesh), and Shabbat as the eternal rest after labor. While the Three Pilgrimage Festivals commemorate overt historical miracles wrought for Israel—the Exodus, the Giving of the Torah, and the Clouds of Glory—Rosh Hashanah commemorates the creation of Man. Seeing that the Sages concluded that \"it were better for man had he not been created\" (Eruvin 13b), why celebrate a festival on the anniversary of his creation? In truth, the essence of every festival is its intrinsic holiness (mikra kodesh), where Israel draws down supernal holiness from on High, shedding worldly burdens to occupy themselves with Torah (Yerushalmi Shabbat 15:3). One who accepts the yoke of Torah casts off the yoke of worldly labor (Avos 3:5), living in a constant state resembling Shabbat and Yom Tov (Raya Mehemna, Tzav 29b; Rambam, Shemittah v'Yovel 13:13). Had Adam not sinned, all Israel would have been priests (\"a kingdom of priests\", Shemos 19:6). The World to Come is \"the day that is entirely Shabbat\" (Tamid 7:4), when physical toil ceases. Even before the Fall, Adam was placed in Gan Eden \"to dress it and to keep it\" (Bereishis 2:15)—interpreted as positive and negative commandments (Zohar I, 27a)—followed by the Sabbath rest (menuchah) to taste the reward of the World to Come. On Shabbat all creative work is prohibited, even food preparation (ochel nefesh), for \"he who toiled on the eve of Shabbat shall eat on Shabbat\" (Avodah Zarah 3a)."

        {
          "h": "The theme: Yom Tov permitting food preparation (ochel nefesh), the six festival days sanctified by Israel, and Yom Kippur as the Shabbat of Shabbats (Shabbat Shabbaton). The experience of Shabbat’s holiness corresponds directly to one's labor during the six workdays. On Yom Tov, however, food preparation (melechet ochel nefesh) is permitted (Beitzah 12a), and physical mitzvos apply—eating Matzah on Pesach, the Lulav and Sukkah on Succos, the Shofar on Rosh Hashanah, and accepting the yoke of all mitzvos on Shavuot. This is because festivals are sanctified by Israel (Yisrael d'kadshinhu) following the expulsion from Eden, when daily labor ceased to be pure spiritual mitzvos. To lift Israel from worldly immersion, Hashem established six festival days across the year: the first and seventh days of Pesach, Shavuot, Rosh Hashanah, the first day of Succos, and Shemini Atzeret. Through these six festival days where labor is restricted solely to sustaining life, holiness is infused into all secular workdays of the year. Yom Kippur is the Shabbat Shabbaton sanctified by Israel, paralleling Shabbat. Prior to the Fall, Shabbat was entirely holy; post-sin, the yetzer hara tarnishes even the Sabbath through excessive worldly indulgence. On Yom Kippur, all sins are atoned and all the holiness of the year's Sabbaths is collected and elevated, transcending even physical food and drink like the World to Come. In Creation, Hashem worked for six days and rested on the seventh; but Adam was created on the sixth day and entered immediately into Shabbat as the first day of his count (Shabbat 69b), establishing that man must first anchor himself in holiness before engaging in the work of the world."

          "h": "The theme: Rosh Hashanah as the eve of Yom Kippur, the creation of the Satan with Chavah, and the Nesirah (severance from back-to-back to face-to-face). In the calendar of festivals sanctified by Israel, the order follows man's vantage. Adam was created on Rosh Hashanah; the first sanctified day of his count was Yom Kippur (the counterpart of Shabbat), followed by six festival days, with Rosh Hashanah serving as the sixth day—the eve of Shabbat (Erev Shabbat), preparing for Yom Kippur (\"and they shall prepare that which they bring in\", Shemos 16:5). Rosh Hashanah prepares for Yom Kippur, the Sabbath of penitents. The First Tablets were given on Shabbat (Shabbat 86b); the Second Tablets, given after the rectification of the golden calf, were given on Yom Kippur, a day of absolute pardon when the Satan has no permission to prosecute (Yoma 20a). The preparation begins with the Shofar of Rosh Hashanah which confounds the Satan at the outset of his accusation (Rosh Hashanah 16b). The Satan was created on Rosh Hashanah alongside Chavah (\"and closed up the flesh instead thereof\", Bereishis 2:21; Bereishis Rabbah 17:6), for accusation stems from immersion in carnal lust. The woman was made an ezer k'negdo—an aid by standing opposite him—for through overcoming opposition and rectifying sin, man reaches a higher summit than the wholly righteous. Creation began with darkness preceding light (breisha chashocha v'hadar nehora, Shabbat 77b); a tzaddik falls seven times and rises (Mishlei 24:16), matching the fall of the seven kings of Edom (Zayin Melachin Kadma'in). Man was initially created androgynous back-to-back (du-partzufin achor b'achor, Berachos 61a) with no vulnerability to external evil; but to bestow and reproduce (amru tzaddik ki tov), the woman was severed (nesirah) to stand face-to-face (panim b'panim). With this separation and the closing of the flesh, the Satan found a foothold in the posterior aspects of the thighs (kav yarech Ya'akov / Netzach, Hod, and Yesod). Adam and Yaakov possessed no shame prior to sin, wearing garments solely to conceal post-sin vulnerability (Shabbat 77b; Ta'anit 5b)."

        {
          "h": "The theme: The fruit of Gan Eden, the creation of the fleshly seal (segirat ha-basar), the Shofar rousing man from slumber, and descent for the sake of ascent. The fruits of Gan Eden (excluding the Tree of Knowledge) were like Manna, fully absorbed into the 248 limbs without requiring bodily excretion. Because man was endowed with free will, and Hashem foresaw that he would transgress, He fashioned for him the \"closing of the flesh\" (segirat ha-basar, Bereishis 2:21). This physiological addition provided a foothold for the unholy outer husks (chitzonim), creating an avenue in creation to act against divine will. This arrived through the fashioning of the woman, who was easily seduced and urged her husband to eat. The Satan, yetzer hara, and Angel of Death were thus created; yet all was for the ultimate good (ezer), for by withstanding temptation man attains a higher summit than the unfallen state. Though Adam was judged and sentenced to death on Rosh Hashanah, his descendants continue the holy chain unto Mashiach, where the penitent ascends higher than Gan Eden. On Rosh Hashanah, the primal holiness of Gan Eden awakens, alongside the deep sleep that triggered the Fall. The remedy is the Shofar, which the Rambam explains: \"Awake, you sleepers, from your slumber!\" (Hilchos Teshuvah 3:4). The yetzer hara was created as a necessary part of existence, associated with the divine Name Havayah Elohim, for continuous unvaried goodness cannot be intensely appreciated without contrast (like the laws of niddah, Niddah 31b). Sluggishness is a descent for the sake of ascent (yeridah l'tzorech aliyah); only when one sinks into spiritual slumber without arousing the fear of Hashem does the yetzer hara drag him into ruin."

        {
          "h": "The theme: The timing of Adam's sin during the six days of Creation, the slaughter of the yetzer hara, and David HaMelech establishing repentance. Adam stumbled by awakening from his slumber to carnal lust. His critical error lay in not preserving his dignity through the first night (\"man abides not in honor\", Tehillim 49:13; Sanhedrin 38b): the six days of Creation established permanent natural laws for all time. Had Adam waited until the Sabbath night when Creation was complete, any subsequent sin would have been a passing accident (mikreh) affecting himself alone. Because he sinned during the six days of Creation, the intensity of the yetzer hara became stamped into the very nature of the human species, adding active incitement (hasatah) to what had previously been mere slackening. Slumber is a physiological necessity (one who vows not to sleep for three days is flogged for a vain oath and sleeps immediately, Nedarim 15a); but through Adam's sin, knowledge of evil was fused into human nature, requiring miraculous divine assistance to overcome it. David HaMelech achieved this by slaying his yetzer through fasting (\"my heart is slain within me\", Tehillim 109:22; Bava Batra 17a), foreshadowing the Future when Hashem will slaughter the yetzer hara (Sukkah 52a). Had his generation been worthy, David would have been the Messiah; but because the generation was imperfect, the yetzer returned as a passing traveler (helech, II Shmuel 12:4; Sukkah 52b) in the incident of Batsheva. David established the yoke of repentance (Avodah Zarah 5a), showing that a single individual who repents brings forgiveness to the entire world (Yoma 86b)."

        {
          "h": "The theme: The Shofar confounding the Satan, the \"Great Shofar\" of Mashiach, and the scapegoat sent to Azazel. The Shofar blows on Rosh Hashanah confound the Satan, who panics thinking the Great Shofar of the redemption has sounded: \"in that day the great shofar shall be blown\" (Yeshayah 27:13). The Shofar shakes the heart (\"shall a horn be blown in a city, and the people not tremble?\", Amos 3:6). The Great Shofar of the End of Days will awaken even the lost and dispersed (ovdim v'nidachim); the Shofar of Rosh Hashanah is an awakening from below (itaruta d'letata) to arouse those slumbering in indifference. When a Jew initiates an awakening even like the eye of a needle (Shir HaShirim Rabbah 5:2), Hashem responds with boundless arousal from Above (itaruta d'le'ila). The accuser panics, fearing that continued prosecution will cause Hashem to pour forth the Great Shofar of Mashiach, wherefore he ceases his accusation. This prepares the way for the total atonement of Yom Kippur, where the scapegoat bears all sins to the wilderness (Vayikra 16:22). The goat (sa'ir) corresponds to \"first darkness\" (breisha chashocha, Shabbat 77b)—as the dark goat leads the flock before the white sheep, and Esav (ish sa'ir) was born before Yaakov. Night was created for sleep (Eruvin 65a); Adam fell into slumber to attain the radiant primordial light, but sin deepened the night into the darkness of exile (\"darkness shall cover the earth\", Yeshayah 60:2). The scapegoat sent to Azazel atones for the fallen angels Uzza and Azael (Yoma 67b), who fell through carnal desire (the seeing eye and coveting heart), obscuring the true primordial light sown for the righteous (or zaru'a la-tzaddik)."

        {
          "h": "The theme: Israel as stars and the moon, the washing of the blackness, and the vision of Yitzchak at the Binding. Israel is compared to stars (Bamidbar Rabbah 2:13) and reckons by the moon (Sukkah 29a), illuminating the night. Israel inherits the \"land of the living\" (eretz ha-chayim) which is the opposite of the \"solitary land\" (eretz gezerah); their true will is to perform Hashem's will, thwarted only by the yeast in the dough (Berachos 17a). Midrash Shir HaShirim Rabbah (1:5) expounds: \"Look not upon me, because I am blackish—with a little laundering we are cleansed\"; the heathen are essentially dark from their mother's womb, whereas Israel is an actual portion of God from the realm of light, where a small ray of light expels much darkness. This is the festival of Rosh Hashanah: \"at the concealed moon (ba-keseh) for our feast day\" (Tehillim 81:4): \"though I sit in darkness, Hashem shall be a light unto me\" (Michah 7:8) through the candle of mitzvah and the light of Torah (Mishlei 6:23). In this world mortal man cannot see Hashem and live (Shemos 33:20); even ministering angels do not behold Him, yet tzaddikim behold Him at death (Bamidbar Rabbah 19:3). At the end of Ta'anit (31a) the Sages state that in the Future each tzaddik will point with his finger, saying: \"Behold, this is our God\" (Yeshayah 25:9); in Shabbat (89b), Yitzchak points out the Holy One to their eyes. Yitzchak merited this vision at the Binding of Isaac (Akeidah), causing his physical eyes to dim from worldly sight (Bereishis Rabbah 65:10), the blind being accounted as dead (Nedarim 64b). Rosh Hashanah is called the second day (yoma tinyana), belonging to the side of Yitzchak (Gevurah / Judgment). Gevurah (גבורה = 216) equals Re'iyah (ראיה = 216 = sight), sharing the letters of Yir'ah (יראה = awe); by guarding one's eyes from filthy lusts, one merits divine awe and holy vision."

          "h": "The theme: Guarding the eyes as the archetype of overcoming sin, hearing vs. seeing, and the Patriarchs rectifying Adam's Fall. The primary safeguard against transgression is averting the initial gaze of the eye, which is the inception of all sin, as demonstrated by the primordial sin of Adam and Chavah which serves as the archetype (binyan av) for all generational iniquities. That first sin cast darkness upon the world, causing holy vision to depart and leaving only hearing (shemi'ah), which functions even in the dark. Hashem made His voice heard in the Garden (Bereishis 3:8) so that man might repent through hearing; had Adam repented then, darkness would have dissolved and holy vision would have been restored. At Sinai, Israel began the rectification of the Fall (\"I said: You are godlike... but you shall die like Adam\", Tehillim 82:6–7), hearing the divine voice and living (Devarim 4:33). They were drawn after the voice until their vision was healed, meriting to \"see the voices\" (ro'im et ha-kolot, Shemos 20:15)—perceiving spiritual realities with the eyes. When Adam heard Hashem in the Garden, great dread fell upon him, but instead of repenting, one sin dragged another (Avos 4:2): seeing himself in darkness, he foolishly imagined that he was hidden from Hashem (\"can any hide himself in secret places that I shall not see him?\", Yirmiyah 23:24; Tehillim 139:8), damaging his faith (emunah), whereupon his death sentence was sealed. The Patriarchs came to rectify Adam's Fall: Avraham rectified the root flaw of faith (\"and he believed in Hashem\", Bereishis 15:6); Yitzchak rectified the inception of sin in forbidden sight, having worldly vision removed in his lifetime; and Yaakov rectified the physical act of eating forbidden food, praying: \"and will give me bread to eat\" (Bereishis 28:20)—eating solely what Hashem bestows upon him!"

                  "text": "Beitzah 16a: ‘A person’s entire livelihood is allocated to him during the period from Rosh HaShana to Yom Kippur. During that time, as each individual is judged, it is decreed exactly how much money he will earn for all his expenditures of the coming year, except for expenditures for Shabbatot, and expenditures for Festivals, and expenditures for the school fees of his sons’ Torah study. In these areas, no exact amount is determined at the beginning of the year; rather, if he reduced the amount he spends for these purposes, his income is reduced and he earns that much less money in that year, and if he increased his expenditures in these areas, his income is increased to ensure that he can cover the expense. Therefore, one may borrow for these purposes, since he is guaranteed to have enough income to cover whatever he spends for them.’",

In these areas, no exact amount is determined at the beginning of the year; rather, if he reduced the amount he spends for these purposes, his income is reduced and he earns that much less money in that year, and if he increased his expenditures in these areas, his income is increased to ensure that he can cover the expense.         {
          "h": "The theme: Purim as \"feasting and gladness\" (mishteh v'simchah), feasting as the vehicle of human attachment, and Lot's rescue through Avraham's merit. Purim is uniquely designated as days of \"feasting and gladness\" because Israel accepted the feast and rejoicing upon themselves rather than a work-prohibited festival (Megillah 5b). The core obligation is the feast, where one must drink ad d'lo yada (Megillah 7b). The inception of the peril arose through dining at Ahasuerus's banquet (Megillah 12a), the cure before the blow was seeded through the king's wine-merry heart (Esther 1:10), and the salvation culminated through Esther's banquets. Feasting serves as the primary instrument of social bonding, love, and friendship. Just as gentile bread and wine were prohibited to prevent intermarriage (Shabbat 17b) and seduction never occurs without eating and drinking (Chullin 4b), so holy feasting unites hearts. The first banquet recorded in the Torah was Lot's feast for the angels (Bereishis 19:3), through which he was saved. Although Lot was delivered in the merit of Avraham, a merit saves another only when the beneficiary absorbs an impression of that righteousness through personal attachment, as \"a son confers merit upon a father\" (Sanhedrin 104a). Lot absorbed Avraham's trait of hospitality (hachnasat orchim), which is rooted in love. There are three holy loves: the love of Hashem (exclusive to Israel, His beloved companion); the love of Torah (the exclusive heritage of Jacob); and the love of Israel, which encompasses the love of all creations (\"love the creations and draw them near to Torah\", Avos 1:12). This unity must not become an unholy conspiracy of the wicked, for while assembling is good for the righteous, scattering is beneficial for the wicked (Sanhedrin 71b). The Generation of the Dispersion (Dor HaPalagah) were united in absolute harmony, yet their unity brought about universal linguistic division; nevertheless, they were spared the total annihilation of the Flood on account of the peaceful harmony among them (Bereishis Rabbah 38:6)."

        {
          "h": "The theme: The three camps of Israel matching the three loves, and the expulsion of the metzora, the zav, and the tamei meit. The dawn of Avraham Avinu’s light marked the foundation of Knesset Israel, divided into three sacred camps corresponding to the three loves. The Camp of the Shechinah (Machaneh Shechinah) embodies the consummate love of Hashem; one defiled by a corpse (tamei meit) is expelled from there (Pesachim 67a), for physical death signifies the temporary absence of absolute attachment to the Living God. Only Torah scholars whose flesh is holy fire can cleave to this devouring fire (Chagigah 27a). The Camp of the Levites (Machaneh Leviyah) embodies the love of Torah; those afflicted with unholy bodily discharges (zavim) are expelled from there, for carnal lust flourishes only in a heart empty of Torah (Rambam, Issurei Biah 22:21; Kiddushin 30b). The Camp of Israel (Machaneh Yisrael) embodies the love of fellow Jews (Ahavat Yisrael), rooted in every Jew from Avraham (\"love your neighbor as yourself is the great principle of the Torah\", Bereishis Rabbah 24:7). Hillel taught the convert: \"What is hateful to you do not do to your fellow—this is the whole Torah\" (Shabbat 31a). From this camp only the leper (metzora) is expelled, having transgressed against fellow humans through evil speech (lashon hara) and narrow-eyed begrudging. Even in the leper, love of Israel remains latently rooted, as demonstrated by the four lepers who delivered Samaria from famine (II Melachim 7). Yet because he manifested hatred in deed, he is banished from walled cities (Pesachim 67a). Walled cities represent the restrained spirit of Knesset Israel, enclosed by the protective fences of the Torah, unlike open cities (arei ha-perazi) or lawless nations. When Israel unites in genuine love, even the foul galbanum blends pleasantly with pure frankincense (chelbenah im levonah, Keritot 6b), and \"Ephraim is joined to idols; let him alone\" (Hoshea 4:17; Bereishis Rabbah 38:6)."

          "h": "The theme: The Three Patriarchs and their banquets, Belshazzar's bread vs. Ahasuerus's wine, and the egalitarian feast. Avraham Avinu is the root of all three loves, but his prominent trait was the love of all creations, planting an orchard (Eshel) in Beersheba to feed and give drink to wayfarers (Sotah 10b). Avraham hosted a banquet on the day Yitzchak was weaned (yom higamel Yitzchak, Bereishis 21:8)—which the Midrash expounds as the day Yitzchak was circumcised (Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer §29; Tosafos, Shabbat 130a). While pagan feasts deteriorate into licentious boasts (Megillah 12b), Avraham's banquet infused the nations with the revulsion of lust through the power of circumcision. Yitzchak corresponds to the love of Torah (Gevurah), the absolute antithesis of lust. Yitzchak made a feast for Abimelech when the Philistines confessed: \"We saw certainly that Hashem was with you\" (Bereishis 26:28), acknowledging that Hashem is the God of Israel. Yet because Yitzchak's bed still contained dross (Esav), he assumed the nations could be fully unified with him; immediately afterward Esav married Canaanite women who grieved Yitzchak and Rivkah (Bereishis 26:34–35). Yaakov Avinu, whose bed was whole and who never died (Ta'anit 5b), cleaved entirely to the Living God (Havayah / Vav / Truth), never hosting a banquet for the nations. He merely attended Laban's feast when Knesset Israel was founded (Bereishis 29:22), and at his family meal Scripture states: \"he called his brethren to eat bread\" (ibid. 31:54), not designating it a mishteh. Belshazzar’s meal was designated after bread (\"made a great feast [lechem rav] to a thousand\", Daniel 5:1), drinking wine alone in royal haughtiness without mingling with his subjects (Megillah 12b). Conversely, Ahasuerus hosted a mishteh aimed at social fraternization (\"according to every man's pleasure\", Esther 1:8). Eating bread sustains individual life; drinking wine represents egalitarian fellowship, joy, and the expansion of vitality."

        {
          "h": "The theme: The future circle dance of the righteous, wine preserved in its grapes, the Serpent's crushed grapes, and the blood of the covenant. In the Future, the righteous will form a circular dance (machol, Ta'anit 31a) around the Holy One; in a circle, every point is equidistant from the center, with none first and none last. The banquet of the Future will feature \"wine preserved in its grapes\" (yayin ha-meshumar b'anavav, Berachos 34b)—a feast unlike anything in this world. In this world, wine brought wailing (yelalah) when Chavah squeezed grapes for Adam (Berachos 40a). Man was made upright, the entire universe forming a single harmonious stature wherein love of fellow creations was natural, like a person loving the limbs of his own body. Wine was created only to comfort mourners (\"give strong drink unto him that is ready to perish, and wine unto those that be of heavy hearts\", Mishlei 31:6; Eruvin 65a). Seeking excessive joy in this world is forbidden as long as Hashem does not rejoice fully in His world; wine was given to reward the wicked in this world to destroy them in the World to Come (Eruvin 65a). Joy and love are one; the Serpent seduced Chavah to squeeze grapes to create an unholy bond with humanity beyond divine design. \"Whoever adds, diminishes\" (Sanhedrin 29a); this excessive joy brought mourning, shame, and enmity between man and the Serpent. This generated holy hatred against evil (\"Do not I hate them, Hashem, that hate You?\", Tehillim 139:21). Opposite this arose the yetzer hara and human discord, from the quarrel of Cain and Abel unto the first murder. This is the root of Esav, who embodies the Serpent's enmity (\"and I will put enmity\", Bereishis 3:15; \"and I hated Esau\", Malachi 1:3), the antithesis of the three holy loves. Yechezkel declared: \"since you have not hated blood, therefore blood shall pursue you\" (Yechezkel 35:6)—referring to the blood of the Paschal offering, the blood of circumcision, and human blood within the body. The blood of Pesach awakens the love of Hashem Who passed over our homes; the blood of circumcision distinguishes Israel from the uncircumcised nations, manifesting the love of Torah which the nations rejected (Avodah Zarah 2b). The foreskin represents superfluous lust; Adam was created circumcised (Avot d'Rabbi Natan §2), but through his sin drew forward his foreskin (Sanhedrin 38b), transmitting congenital uncircumcision to his offspring. Avraham was the first to be circumcised, rectifying Adam's Fall through consummate love, and fathered Yitzchak who was circumcised on the eighth day!"

        {
          "h": "The theme: The side of Gevurah rejecting superfluities, Yaakov's consummate simplicity (temimut), and eating bread versus feasting. The side of Gevurah distances lusts and luxuries, for \"the Torah went forth from its side\" (Zohar II, 84b), which Esav detested along with the blood of man within his body (hatred of fellow creations). Preeminently, Esav hated Yaakov, the \"wholehearted man\" (ish tam, Bereishis 25:27), for \"men of blood hate the wholehearted\" (Mishlei 29:10). Simplicity means existing solely with Hashem (\"You shall be wholehearted with Hashem your God\", Devarim 18:13), asking for nothing beyond what He provides, like a wife looking up to her husband. Through this, Yaakov's bed was unblemished, forming one indivisible nation, for bodily severance is death. Yaakov never died (Ta'anit 5b); his burial was merely an optical perception of this world. When Yaakov sought to dwell in serenity, assuming the time of the End had arrived, the turmoil of Yosef sprang upon him (Rashi on Bereishis 37:2), fearing that the holy covenant (Yesod) was lost among the nations. Circumcision demands simplicity: \"walk before Me, and be wholehearted\" (Bereishis 17:1), casting off superfluities. Yaakov asked solely for \"bread to eat and raiment to put on\" (Bereishis 28:20); his meal was called \"eating bread\" and not a mishteh, for a feast implies seeking superfluous joy and equality, whereas Yaakov is the Patriarch who channels life unto his children. Yisro's meal was likewise designated \"to eat bread\" (Shemos 18:12), abandoning worldly heights for the wilderness to study Torah, whose way is \"a morsel with salt you shall eat\" (Avos 6:4). As a proselyte, Yisro felt the hierarchical divisions of Torah, establishing chiefs of thousands and hundreds. All this applies before the ultimate rectification; when Hashem rejoices in His works, He will bestow the concealed wine (yayin ha-meshumar b'anavav, Berachos 34b)."
