        {
          "h": "The theme: Yaakov dwelling in serenity, aged wine gladdening the elders, and the Generation of the Dispersion. When Yaakov sought to dwell in serenity, Hashem replied: \"Is it not enough for the righteous what is prepared for them in the World to Come?\" (Rashi on Bereishis 37:2). Following the sale of Yosef, the brothers and Yosef drank no wine (Bereishis Rabbah 92:5) until they reunited in Egypt (\"and they drank, and were merry with him\", Bereishis 43:34), like one who abstains from wine upon seeing degradation (Sotah 2a). Upon reuniting, Yosef sent his father \"old wine that satisfies the mind of the aged\" (Megillah 16b)—wine preserved in its grapes, tasting the World to Come in this life (Berachos 17a). Yaakov lived seventeen years in Egypt free from sorrow and the yetzer hara (Tanna D'vei Eliyahu Rabbah, ch. 5), meriting serenity in life because his bed was whole. Tzaddikim taste this reward before death (Shemos Rabbah 52:3), but Yaakov attained it in life. Yitzchak tasted this wine through Yaakov when receiving the blessings, contrasting with the wine of Esav that brings lamentation. Avraham’s great feast at Yitzchak's weaning prefigured the banquet of the Future when Hashem repays kindness to Yitzchak's seed (Pesachim 119b). Avraham’s light began during the Generation of the Dispersion (Dor HaPalagah)—the darkness preceding light—who sought love among friends to be \"one people\" (Bereishis 11:6), but severed themselves from Hashem. Unity cannot exist below when detached from Hashem; without Him, human societies fragment into conflict. Avraham knew the Oneness of Hashem, meriting love of creations (\"the entire world was created to accompany him\", Berachos 6b). The builders of the Tower mimicked love like an ape before man; their city and tower became the instrument of their dispersal, for their union was rooted in carnal lust."

          "h": "The theme: Lot's lusts, the division of Ammon and Moab, and Sodom's gold versus the Foundation Stone (Even Shetiyah). Lot accompanied Avraham assuming he possessed love of creations, but inwardly was filled with lust. When he acquired wealth to fulfill his passions, strife erupted between their herdsmen (Bereishis 13:7). Avraham told him: \"Separate yourself, I pray you, from me\" (ibid. 13:9), for Lot hated Israel: Ammon and Moab became the \"evil neighbors of Jerusalem\" (Sanhedrin 96b; Nazir 23b). Lot was completely severed from Israel on the male side (\"an Ammonite or Moabite shall not enter into the congregation of Hashem\", Devarim 23:4); but their females were permitted immediately (Yevamos 69a) through the \"two good doves\" (shtei peridot tovot, Bava Kamma 38b)—Ruth the Moabitess and Naamah the Ammonitess. Lot's daughters acted for the sake of Heaven (Bereishis Rabbah 51:8), and Hashem provided wine in the cave carrying the potency of the wine preserved in its grapes, to bring forth the root of Mashiach: \"I have found David My servant—where did I find him? In Sodom\" (Bereishis Rabbah 41:4). In the Future, Sodom and her daughters will return to their former state (Yechezkel 16:55). The angels who announced Yitzchak's birth—the foundation of Israel as \"one nation\"—were the same angels sent to overturn Sodom, the darkness preceding light. Sodom sought to abolish hospitality, imagining themselves unique. Gold was created solely for the Holy Temple (Shemos Rabbah 35:1), for this world cannot bear such luxury; yet Sodom possessed dust of gold (Iyov 28:6) because the root of Mashiach was hidden there. The Temple rests on the Foundation Stone (Even Shetiyah) whence the world was founded; the cities of Sodom were established upon a single rock (Bereishis Rabbah 51:5) parallel to the Even Shetiyah. Israel on its land channels divine vitality to all nations (the seventy festival bulls atoning for seventy nations, Sukkah 55b). The prophets wept over the downfall of the nations; but when Hashem bestows abundance upon the nations directly, they kick (Devarim 32:15). In Sodom, ultimate luxury was inverted into cruelty, seeking the destruction of the world, wherefore they were overturned and destroyed."

          "h": "The theme: Lot's rescue on Passover night, the wine of the angels, and the extraction of the spark of Mashiach through drunkenness. Lot was saved in the merit of Avraham which illuminated him when he walked with him, enabling him to father daughters whose inward intention was for Heaven. Although Lot separated from Avraham and joined the men of Sodom, the ancestral root in the depths of his heart remained. When the angels arrived, kind found its kind (matza min et mino): the dormant spark within Lot awakened to host them at a banquet. This occurred on Passover night (Bereishis Rabbah 50:12)—the season awakening Hashem's love—commanding the Four Cups of wine, which gladden rather than intoxicate (the intoxicating drops being spilled during the Ten Plagues). The wine of Lot's banquet was wine from heaven (yayin ha-meshumar b'anavav), just as the Manna was bread of the angels (Yoma 76a), and the matzot he baked carried the taste of Manna. Through this banquet Lot bonded with the angels, dispelling darkness for that hour, like the temporary illumination at the Exodus. Returning to his base nature, Lot became intoxicated in the cave; yet through that holy residual wine, he fathered the root of Mashiach specifically in his drunkenness. The holy spark could be extracted from him only when conscious intellect (Da'as) was entirely removed, for consciously Lot was submerged in defilement. Had he retained any conscious awareness, the evil of the Tree of Knowledge would have overpowered the holy spark, fulfilling: \"a time wherein one man rules over another to his own hurt\" (Koheles 8:9). Lot's drunkenness was to his personal hurt—his male descendants being barred from Israel—while the holy spark of David HaMelech emerged from the celestial wine provided in the cave!"

The king said: ‘If I punish them in the presence of the nobleman, they would then say: Had the country-dweller been here, he would have protected us. And if it would be [that I punish them] in the presence of the country-dweller, they would then say: Had the nobleman been here, he would have protected us.…’"
